title: Preface
summary: Front matter of CIA 'Studies in Intelligence' (Vol. 11, No. 1, Winter 1967), approved for release 2019/10/07. Covers the journal's editorial policy: articles may address any theoretical, doctrinal, operational, or historical intelligence topic, accepted if the Editorial Board judges they contribute to intelligence literature. Lists the editor (Penn K. Edwards) and Editorial Board members (Sherman Kent, chairman, and others). Includes one featured article title: getting factory markings from inside a Soviet upper-stage space vehicle.

title: THE KIDNAPING OF THE LUNIK

nodes.title: On View Abroad
nodes.summary: A declassified CIA-era account of a Soviet industrial exhibition tour abroad, which displayed a Lunik space vehicle stage. U.S. intelligence borrowed it overnight, found it was a production item with engine and electronics removed, and examined its performance, structure, wiring, and engine size. Analysts then sought to read factory markings to identify the manufacturing plant, since earlier copies were insufficiently detailed, prompting another access attempt.

nodes.title: Plans and Problems
nodes.summary: A CIA-linked team planned to intercept the Lunik crate, a suspected Soviet lunar probe disguised as 'models of astronomic apparatus' shipped with a trade exhibition. Early access at the exhibition was blocked by logistics and a 24-hour Soviet guard, so the plan shifted to the post-show transport. The team (four specialists from the Joint Factory Markings Center) prepared local clothing, photographic gear, and tools, after the Station photographed the crate, which was bolted shut from inside so entry had to be through the roof. Rail interception was rejected for lack of capability, leaving the truck run from the grounds to the station as the viable option.

nodes.title: Lunik on Loan
nodes.summary: A declassified account of a covert operation to access the Soviet Lunik probe after an exhibition. The Lunik was secretly trucked from the fair grounds to a walled salvage yard, avoiding Soviet surveillance, while a Soviet checker and his hotel-bound driver were kept out of the way. Photographers and markings teams opened the crate at night, photographed the payload orb and engine compartment, cut and later replaced a sealed wire, and took two couplings for analysis.

nodes.title: Returned in Good Condition
nodes.summary: Describes the covert retrieval of a Soviet Lunik space probe stage: reassembling the orb in its basket through a difficult hour-long procedure, securing wires, inspecting for evidence, replacing crate parts, and having the truck returned and loaded onto a rail flatcar. The Soviets apparently never learned the Lunik was borrowed. Analysis yielded a Markings Center Brief (MCB 60-1) identifying the producer, that it was the fifth stage built, three electrical component suppliers, and the Soviet part-numbering system. The text stresses the lasting value of cooperation between covert operators and overt collectors.

summary: A declassified CIA-era account of covertly accessing a Soviet Lunik probe stage shown at a foreign trade exhibition. U.S. intelligence borrowed it overnight, found a production item, and sought factory markings. Planning, a truck interception from the grounds to a salvage yard, night crate opening, photography, wire cutting, and coupling samples followed. The stage was reassembled, returned unnoticed, and analyzed, yielding MCB 60-1 on producer, build number, suppliers, and part numbering, stressing covert-overt cooperation.
